newsitem.title: USA: Republicans make peace with leaders, show unity.
newsitem.headline: Republicans make peace with leaders, show unity.

text.p: House Republicans made their peace Wednesday night with party leaders who led them through weeks of bitter public feuding and ugly recriminations involving a plot to oust House Speaker Newt Gingrich.
Gingrich's top deputies apologised for their mistakes before nearly all 228 Republicans in an extraordinary and emotional three-hour meeting.
No vote of confidence was taken, but Representative Kenny Hulshof of Missouri told reporters, "If we had taken a vote, you would have had a unanimous vote for the leadership team."
The third-in-command, Republican Whip Tom DeLay of Texas, admitted he erred in telling a group of rebels he would take their side against the embattled speaker, several lawmakers said.

The lawmakers said they forgave him and accepted his explanation that he had been physically exhausted by legislative battles and went overboard in an attempt to emphathize with their complaints against the speaker.
But his spokesman John Feehery emphasised to reporters that DeLay was not the only one who admitted his mistakes in the closed door party meeting.

Majority Leader Dick Armey of Texas denied any role in the aborted coup, as he had said in public. Republican Conference Chairman John Boehner of Ohio had said earlier he had been unaware of the plot.

The former Republican Leadership Chairman Bill Paxon of New York admitted to mistakes of participating in the talks with dissidents. Hand-picked by Gingrich to be on the Republican team, he was forced to resign his post last week after he said he had lost the confidence and trust of the speaker.
But he received a standing ovation Wednesday night and there was some talk that he might be restored to his post.
Lawmakers said the leaders did not contradict each other's stories or attempt to assign blame.
Gingrich set a tone of forgiveness by opening the meeting with a biblical verse, Romans 12:14-21, which begins "Bless those who persecute you and do not curse them."
At the end, the Republicans passed a resolution pledging unity with the current leadership team and emerged from the Capitol basement conference room laughing and shouting, "228 united Republicans."

"Everybody's upbeat and no one's going to make comments to the contrary," said Representative Mark Souder of Indiana, one of those who had been displeased with Gingrich's handling of legislative fights with President Clinton and the Democrats.
"It was wonderful. It was fabulous," Gingrich said of the conference. Asked how he would show renewed vigour of his leadership he replied, "by passing the tax bill and balancing the budget."

Earlier in the day, Gingrich had asserted his authority in telling them, "I'm the speaker and I'm in charge" and had urged them to put the "tiresome and overwrought saga" behind them and get back to work.

Republican unrest grew this year as the party returned from the 1996 elections with a narrowed majority in the House and less political leverage to use in talks with Clinton on crucial budget and tax issues.
This has proved particularly disturbing to a group of conservatives, many of whom were swept to power in 1994 when the party reclaimed the majority after 40 years.

The embattled speaker narrowly won re-election to his position in January and was reprimanded and fined by his colleagues for ethics violations. Many of the dissidents were particularly upset with his handling of a disaster aid bill in late spring and their belief that he handed the president another public relations victory.

The political intrigue deepened earlier this month when a group of conservative dissidents said they were given reason to believe their effort to oust the speaker would have support from some in the leadership. Several of them mentioned a role played by Republican Whip Tom DeLay of Texas.

Before the meeting, several lawmakers doubted the strife could be ended so easily. One of those, Representative Ray LaHood of Illinois, said the discussion had changed his mind: "I trust the leadership implicitly -- all of them."
